final_query:
MATCH (ah:AccountHolder)-[:HAS_ADDRESS]->(a:Address)
MATCH (ah:AccountHolder)-[:HAS_CREDITCARD]->(cc:CreditCard)
WHERE a.state = 'Washington' AND cc.latePayments > 0.0
RETURN DISTINCT ah.UniqueId AS UniqueId, ah.fullName AS fullName, ah.birthDate AS birthDate
ORDER BY UniqueId

critique.feedback: The first MATCH chain (ah:AccountHolder)-[:HAS_ADDRESS]->(a:Address)-[:HAS_CREDITCARD]->(cc:CreditCard) is wrong: the schema defines HAS_CREDITCARD only as AccountHolder->CreditCard, so there is no Address->HAS_CREDITCARD->CreditCard edge. That pattern eliminates every row (empty result), which contradicts the intended grain of one row per qualifying AccountHolder. Drop that hop and express the two conditions as two independent patterns anchored on the same holder: MATCH (ah:AccountHolder)-[:HAS_ADDRESS]->(a:Address) and MATCH (ah:AccountHolder)-[:HAS_CREDITCARD]->(cc:CreditCard), keeping the existing WHERE a.state = 'Washington' AND cc.latePayments > 0.0 (Address.state and CreditCard.latePayments are the correct property owners, so those reads are fine). Secondarily, RETURN DISTINCT ah.fullName, ah.birthDate collapses distinct AccountHolder identities that share a name and birthDate, while a single holder with multiple Washington addresses or multiple qualifying cards would still fan out before the DISTINCT; since AccountHolder carries UniqueId, project ah.UniqueId (plus fullName/birthDate) or aggregate per holder so the output grain matches 'all AccountHolders'.
